1282.title: Takht Patna Sahib
1282.hook: at Patna, where the Tenth Guru was born
1282.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Takht Patna Sahib to honor the Tenth Guru's birthplace, and the gurdwara keeps items remembered from his childhood for pilgrims to see.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo, where the Granth was completed. Your line was the guru's rest.

A birth certificate holds a town, a date and two names. It doesn't hold the river outside the window, or the sound of the street, or who was carrying the baby when the visitors came. Sikhs remember the Tenth Guru's birth through a place. Far to the east of Punjab, in the city of Patna, near the wide Ganges, a gurdwara stands where tradition says Guru Gobind Singh was born. It's one of the Takhts, the seats of authority. The others you've met sit in Punjab. This one sits a long way off, because his life began far from where most of his story would be told.
screen: `A CERTIFICATE HOLDS A TOWN.` → `PATNA, BY THE GANGES.` → `A TAKHT FAR FROM PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Early on this path, you met the boy by the river. Now, the seat built on his childhood. First, why the family was there at all. Tradition says the Ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was traveling in the east, and his family stayed in Patna while he went on. So the boy was born while his father was away on the road. His childhood name, tradition says, was Gobind Rai. Then the stories the community keeps, and tells warmly. A boy by the river, organizing other children into games of mock battle. A boy the neighbors loved. A woman in the town with no child of her own, who longed to hold him, and gave him food and care. Then the turn. The family went west to Punjab, and his life moved through Anandpur, battle, loss and the founding of the Khalsa. Patna stayed behind as the place of the beginning. That's what sets this Takht apart. Akal Takht faces the Harmandir. Keshgarh marks where the Khalsa was born. Damdama marks where the Granth was completed. Patna marks something smaller and more ordinary: a birth, and a little boy's first years. Its full name is Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib. Sikhs travel there to stand where he was a child, and visitors are shown things kept in memory of his childhood. A seat of authority, built on a nursery.

segments.voice: Picture a wide, slow river with a bank of mud and steps, and a small barefoot boy there among other children, loud and busy with some game. Nobody watching knows yet what his life will hold, so let him just be a child. If you like, let your mind drift to the first river, street or yard you remember from when you were small.
Takht Patna Sahib. The seat of authority in Patna, in the east, built where tradition says Guru Gobind Singh was born and spent his first years. Today's word.
Your line: where he was born. A great life starts as an ordinary childhood by a river. See you tomorrow.

1283.title: Takht Hazur Sahib
1283.hook: at Nanded, where he passed the Guruship to the Granth
1283.howItsDone: Sikhs travel to Hazur Sahib in Nanded to bow where tradition says Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Patna Sahib, by the Ganges in the east. Your line was where he was born.

Draw a line on a map of India. Start at Patna in the east, where the Tenth Guru was born. Swing it west to Anandpur in the hills of Punjab, where the Khalsa began. Then drop it a long way south, across the middle of the country, to a town on the Godavari river called Nanded. The line of his life ends far from where it started, and far from where most of his story happened. You've stood at Nanded once before on this path, for his last days. Now, the place itself, and the Takht that stands there.
screen: `PATNA, ANANDPUR, NANDED.` → `A LIFE DRAWN ACROSS A MAP.` → `IT ENDS IN THE SOUTH.`

segments.voice: Takht Hazur Sahib stands at Nanded, by the Godavari. Hazur is a word of respect for being in the presence of someone great, and Sikhs often call the place simply Hazur Sahib. Its fuller name speaks of Sachkhand, the realm of truth, and Abchal Nagar, which Sikhs render as the steady, unmoving city. Now the history it keeps. Tradition says that here, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh named no person to follow him. He bowed before the Granth and passed the Guruship to it. From that day, Sikhs say, the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa gathered before it as the Guru Panth. So Patna holds the beginning of one life, and Nanded holds its end, and the beginning of something without an end. A person is born, and a person dies. The Granth was given to stay. That's why Sikhs speak of this Takht with such weight: it marks the hand-off. It also shows how far the panth reaches. Patna in the east and Nanded in the south both sit far from Punjab, which some readers take as a quiet reminder that the Guru's house was never meant to belong to one province. Pilgrims come by train and bus from all over to bow where the hand-off happened.

segments.voice: Picture a wide river moving slowly through flat land under a big southern sky, and let the water pass you without hurrying. A river can't be held in one place; it goes on after anyone who stands beside it. If you pray, rest in the Guru's presence by the water; if you don't, let the river carry your breath along.
Takht Hazur Sahib. The seat of authority at Nanded, by the Godavari, where tradition says the Tenth Guru passed the Guruship to the Granth. Today's word.
Your line: where he gave the guruship. A life ended at Nanded, and the Guru stayed, in the Granth. Same time tomorrow.

1284.title: The Sarbat Khalsa
1284.hook: a gathering of the whole panth, rare today and much discussed
1284.howItsDone: A Sarbat Khalsa is a gathering of the Sikh community before the Guru Granth Sahib to pass a gurmatta, a binding resolution; gatherings under this name are rare today and their authority is debated among Sikhs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Hazur Sahib at Nanded, by the Godavari. Your line was where he gave the guruship.

Who gets a say? A family planning a wedding finds out fast. So does a band choosing its name, or a club picking a captain. Somebody always asks: did everyone get asked, or just the loud ones? Behind the Takhts, and the five Sikhs who decide for the community, stands a bigger idea. What if, for the gravest questions, the whole panth came together in one place, in the Guru's presence, and decided as one? Sikhs have a name for that gathering. It's old, it's rare today, and Sikhs argue about it with real feeling.
screen: `WHO GETS A SAY?` → `THE TAKHTS AND THE FIVE.` → `WHAT IF EVERYONE CAME?`

segments.voice: The name is Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat means all, the whole of something. Sikhs hear the same word each time the Ardas, the common prayer, closes by asking for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. So Sarbat Khalsa is the whole Khalsa: all of us together. Now the history, told carefully. Sikh histories describe a time after the Tenth Guru when Sikh bands were scattered and often hunted, and their leaders would meet at Amritsar at festival times; you met those meetings earlier on this path. Tradition says they gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib, talked through what faced them, and made a gurmatta, a resolution taken in the Guru's presence. Once made, it was meant to bind everyone, even those who had argued against it. That's the idea at its best: no single ruler, no single family, but the gathered panth and the Guru together. Then the hard part. Who calls a Sarbat Khalsa today? Who counts as the whole, when Sikhs live in many countries and belong to many organizations? When gatherings have been called under this name in recent times, Sikhs have disagreed, sometimes sharply, about whether they truly spoke for all. Some hold that the Akal Takht should call it. Some want new ways for distant Sikhs to take part. Some think the old form fits the old days best. This path won't settle it. Under the argument sits the hope inside the word: that the Guru's community can still decide as one.

1285.title: The old rehatnamas
1285.hook: earlier codes differ in detail; the 1950 code is the shared reference
1285.howItsDone: Sikh scholars study the older rehatnamas alongside the Sikh Rehat Maryada, which serves as the shared reference for Sikh conduct today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sarbat Khalsa: the whole panth gathered to decide as one. Your line was all of us together.

Two recipe cards for the same dish. One in a grandmother's hand, splattered, with a note in the margin. One printed in a community cookbook, neat and measured. One says a handful and the other says a cup, and one adds a spice the other never mentions. Which is right? Families have that argument at holiday tables. Sikhs have a version of it too, written down over generations. Before the shared code this path has been reading, there were older ones, and they don't all say the same thing.
screen: `TWO CARDS, ONE DISH.` → `A HANDFUL OR A CUP?` → `AN OLDER SHELF OF CODES.`

segments.voice: A rehatnama is a writing about rehat, the Sikh way of living. In the generations after the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote several. Some carry the names of people tradition places near the Guru, such as the poet Bhai Nand Lal. They set out how a Sikh should rise, pray, dress, eat and treat others. Side by side, they share a lot of ground: remember the Name, keep the hair, live honestly, share. Read closely, they differ. One stresses a rule another leaves out. Some carry the worries and the language of their own time and place. Who wrote which parts, and when, is still discussed. So, much later, Sikh bodies worked together to agree on one shared code, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee; you met its writing earlier on this path. Today it's the shared reference gurdwaras point to, though some groups and some historic places keep customs of their own beside it. Here's the turn. A code is the community's best written understanding of how to live the Guru's way, and its wording can change from one era to the next. The Guru it follows does not. The Guru Granth Sahib is fixed, word for word, and every code, old or new, is measured against it, never the other way round.

The old rehatnamas. Earlier writings on the Sikh way of life, sharing much and differing in detail, before the shared code was agreed. Today's word.

1286.title: Why a written code
1286.hook: a shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike
1286.howItsDone: Gurdwaras in different countries follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada for daily prayers, ceremonies and conduct, so a Sikh visiting a gurdwara far from home recognizes the order of things.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old rehatnamas: earlier codes that share much and differ in detail. Your line was codes change, the guru doesn't.

A woman lands in a city she has never seen, tired, far from her family. She finds a gurdwara on a side street and doesn't know a single person inside. But at the door she already knows what to do. Shoes off. Head covered. Into the hall, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, sit with the sangat. Later, down to the langar, where she sits on the floor in a row with strangers and is fed. Nobody had to explain any of it. How does that happen, and why did Sikhs bother to write it down?
screen: `A STRANGER IN A NEW CITY.` → `SHE ALREADY KNOWS WHAT TO DO.` → `WHY WRITE IT DOWN?`

segments.voice: Four reasons. First, a written code travels. Spoken custom stays close to the village it grew in. A page can cross an ocean, be read in a new language, be taught in a basement class in a city the Gurus never saw. So Sikh families in two countries can open the same pages and find the same daily prayers, the same order for a wedding, the same form for the Ardas. One code, many homes. Second, it settles things more fairly. When two people disagree about how something should be done, they can point to a page instead of to whoever speaks loudest or has the most money. A rule on paper applies to the powerful and the poor alike. Third, it gives the newcomer a starting place. Someone learning the path, or coming back after years away, can read what is asked instead of guessing or feeling foolish. Fourth, it keeps the community in conversation. The shared code was agreed by Sikhs working together, and the Guru Panth can still discuss it. A written code doesn't replace the Guru, or love, or seva, or the remembrance of the Name. It's more like a common doorway. Families still bring their own warmth, their own food, their own way of laughing in the langar line. But the doorway is the same width wherever you find it, and anyone can walk through.
screen: `A PAGE CAN CROSS AN OCEAN.` · `POINT TO A PAGE, NOT A VOICE.` · `A STARTING PLACE FOR NEWCOMERS.` · `A COMMON DOORWAY, NOT THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE CODE, MANY HOMES.`

segments.voice: Choose one rule your household keeps that nobody ever wrote down: shoes at the door, who sits where, what gets said before a meal. Put it into one plain sentence, the way it would read for someone who just moved in, on paper or silently. Then sit with it and ask whether the sentence holds everything the habit does.
Why a written code. A shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Today's word.

1287.title: Caring for kesh
1287.hook: washing, combing and covering the hair as daily care
1287.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep kesh wash, comb and cover their hair as part of the daily routine, often in the early morning before prayer, using the kangha kept in the hair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why a written code: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Your line was one code, many homes.

Early morning in a Sikh home. Someone sits on the edge of a bed, long hair down past the shoulders, still damp. A small wooden comb works through it from the ends up, one knot at a time. Then the hair is twisted, wound into a knot on top of the head, and covered. Outside that room, people mostly notice only the last step. Early on this path you met kesh, uncut hair kept as it was made, one of the five Ks. Today isn't the rule. It's the morning.
screen: `DAMP HAIR, A WOODEN COMB.` → `TWISTED, KNOTTED, COVERED.` → `NOT THE RULE: THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code asks Sikhs to keep the hair uncut, and Sikhs speak of it as a gift kept as it was given. But keeping is a verb, and it has three parts. Washing comes first. Long hair is washed and dried with care, often as part of the early-morning bath before prayer, so the body is clean when the mind turns to the Name. Combing comes second. The kangha, the small comb, is itself one of the five Ks, kept in the hair so it can be used any time of day. The code asks Sikhs to comb the hair, and some say a prayer or recite while they comb, so tending the hair and remembering God happen together. Covering comes third. The hair is gathered up and covered, with a turban, a keski, a chunni or another covering, kept clean and kept in honor. Notice what this does to a rule. Don't cut your hair could be kept by doing nothing at all. Caring for kesh asks for something every single morning. It turns a boundary into a small daily act of attention, and the body into part of the practice. A Sikh doesn't only keep the hair; the hair keeps reminding the Sikh. Each tangle asks for patience. Each covering is a small act of respect. And tomorrow the comb comes out again.
screen: `KEEPING IS A VERB.` · `WASHED BEFORE PRAYER.` · `COMBED WITH THE KANGHA.` · `COVERED, KEPT IN HONOR.` · then, large: `DAILY CARE.`

segments.voice: If a comb or brush is nearby, pick it up; if your hair is short or gone, use your fingers instead. Work slowly from the ends up, and when you meet a knot, don't pull: pause, and work it loose. If you pray, remember God with each stroke; if not, just give your hands your full attention.
Caring for kesh. Washing, combing and covering the uncut hair, as a daily act of care and remembrance. Today's word.
Your line: daily care. A rule that's kept by doing, every morning. Go gently.

1288.title: Styles of turban
1288.hook: many styles, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla
1288.howItsDone: Sikhs tie turbans in many styles, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla, often learning a style from family, and children often begin with a patka.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caring for kesh: washing, combing and covering, every morning. Your line was daily care.

Stand at the door of a big gurdwara on a festival morning and watch the heads come in. A neat, pointed turban in deep navy. A rounded one in bright saffron. A small cloth knotted on a boy's head. A tall, wound turban in dark blue, with a steel emblem fixed at the front. Pink at a wedding. White on an older man. Patterned cloth on a young woman. Same faith, same hall, same Guru at the front. Yesterday ended with the covering; today, the covering itself.
screen: `HEADS AT THE GURDWARA DOOR.` → `NAVY, SAFFRON, WHITE, PINK.` → `ONE IDEA, MANY SHAPES.`

segments.voice: Begin with the everyday one. In Punjabi it's often just called the pagg, and its formal name is dastar: a long strip of cloth, folded and wound around the head in layers, finished neatly. Families and regions tie it differently, one to a sharp peak at the front, another rounder and softer, and people often learn the style of a father, an uncle or a friend. Next, the smaller coverings. A patka is a square of cloth tied over the hair knot, often worn by children before they learn the full turban, and by some for sport. A keski is a shorter turban, worn by some under a larger one, and by some, including some Sikh women who wear a turban, on its own. Then the tall one. The dumalla is wound high and full, sometimes with a steel emblem or small weapons tucked into it. It's closely tied to the Nihangs, the Sikh order known for keeping the old martial dress, and others wear it too. Color is mostly choice: some match a shirt, some wear saffron or blue on festival days, some wear one color for years. Here's what joins them. Earlier on this path, the code asked the turban of Sikh men and left it open to women, and your line was crowned. A crown can be tall or neat, bright or plain, and still be a crown. So the week closes: Patna and Hazur Sahib, the Sarbat Khalsa, the old rehatnamas, why a written code, caring for kesh, and now the turban itself.
screen: `THE PAGG, OR DASTAR.` · `PATKA AND KESKI.` · `THE TALL DUMALLA.` · `TALL OR NEAT, STILL A CROWN.` · then, large: `MANY STYLES, ONE CROWN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the turbans you've seen, on a street, on a screen, at a gurdwara, or look at a few pictures if you can. Notice each one without judging: the shape, the color, the care in the folds. Then notice the person under it, who wound that cloth this morning, layer by layer, with their own hands.
Styles of turban. Many ways to tie it, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla, each one the same crown. Today's word.
Your line: many styles, one crown. Tall or neat, bright or plain, the meaning holds. That's the week.
